title: ChatGPT Stopped Reading Your Blog. It's Reading Your Pricing Page.
subtitle: Ahrefs went through 66.6 million ChatGPT answers. It now skips the sites that summarize and goes to whoever owns the facts. In SaaS, that's the page marketing forgot it had.
body_html:
Picture your content team's proudest asset. "What Is Customer Onboarding? The Ultimate Guide (2026)." 4,000 words, eleven H2s, and a stock photo of people high-fiving near a laptop. It ranked. It got cited. For a while, it was how the internet learned your category existed.

And now ChatGPT walks right past it and asks for your pricing page.

ChatGPT, skipping your 4,000-word guide and asking for whoever owns the actual facts.

Ahem. Welcome to The Overlooked Memo, Issue 04, where I read the 14-minute studies so you get the 4-minute version.

This week's study is from Ahrefs, published October 12. They studied 66.6 million ChatGPT answers from August and September: what it searched, and who it cited. Most coverage went straight for the health angle: PubMed climbed from 64th to 4th among cited domains, WebMD slid from 18th to 79th. Ahrefs' own summary is that ChatGPT "seems to be prioritizing original sources over sites that summarize them."

Look, read that as a SaaS marketer for a second. Who's the WebMD in our world? Hmm. It's us. It's every blog post that summarizes a category, a framework or somebody else's survey.

Two things the coverage skipped

First, most answers don't search at all. Only 14.4% of those responses contained fan-out queries, the background searches ChatGPT runs before it answers. So roughly six answers in seven come straight from what the model already believes about you. What's in the model's head came from years of other people talking about you.

Second, when it does search, it wants the official version. The word "official" showed up in 13.1% of English fan-out queries in September, up from 10.1% in August. "Price" went from 6.0% to 8.9%, a 47% jump in one month. In a separate Ahrefs test, 84.4% of factual questions about pricing, features or company details cited at least one official source. Aah. So when a buyer asks what you cost, ChatGPT goes looking for your number.

And what does it find on most SaaS pricing pages? "Contact sales." A monthly/annual toggle that only shows up after the JavaScript loads. A feature grid saved as a PNG. So it shrugs and borrows an answer from a review site that last checked your pricing in 2023.

ChatGPT on your pricing page, looking for a number.

This is where it bites. The pages ChatGPT trusts most (pricing, docs, the changelog, the security page) are the ones most SaaS teams I've worked with treat as nobody's job. Product owns the docs. Support owns the help center. Finance sort of owns pricing. Marketing owns the blog, which is the one asset getting demoted. I wrote technical docs before I moved into marketing, and not once did anyone invite the docs team to the content planning meeting.

Comparisons play by different rules, by the way. For "A vs B" style prompts, only 46.4% of citations went to official sites, versus 63.4% for factual ones. Third-party reviews and listicles still carry that ground, which is exactly why your competitor's "Us vs Them" page keeps popping up.

Is any of this worth the effort? First Page Sage's September 2026 study says the first brand ChatGPT recommends gets a direct click in 10.3% of answers, while the top footnote citation gets 2.3%. B2B software also had the highest rate of people Googling the brand afterward, at 15.8%. So the prize is getting named, and then surviving the fact-check. Your pricing page is where that fact-check happens, yeah.

What I'd do this week

  • Ask ChatGPT ten boring factual questions about your product: price, seat limits, integrations, SOC 2, trial length. Write down what it gets wrong and where it got it from.

  • Put at least a starting price on the pricing page as real text. If you truly can't, explain how pricing works in plain words.

  • Give your docs and changelog one marketing hour a week. Dates on everything, plain names for features, and no "coming soon" from 2024.

  • Pick your top 10 blog posts. What's in each one that only you could publish? If nothing, add your own product data or stop refreshing it.

What I'm watching

Google, mostly. Ahrefs found on October 2 that AI Overviews now appear on 83% of branded searches, and when they cite someone other than you, it's usually Wikipedia, YouTube or LinkedIn. Two engines, two ideas of who counts as official, and one under-loved pricing page stuck in the middle...

Okay, quick recap. ChatGPT now goes to whoever owns the fact. In SaaS, that's mostly pages marketing never touches. Time to touch them.

Your turn: when did someone in marketing last edit your pricing page or your docs? Hit reply and tell me. Honestly, I'm collecting excuses.

Cheers,

Dheeraj

Stuff I read for this: Ahrefs' ChatGPT query fan-out study (Oct 12, 2026); Search Engine Journal on the same data (Oct 12, 2026); First Page Sage, "ChatGPT Click-Through Rate by Ranking Position" (Sep 2026); Ahrefs, "AI Overviews Currently Appear for 83% of Branded Searches" (Oct 2, 2026); MarketingProfs AI Update (Oct 16, 2026).

title: ChatGPT Just Gave You 300 Characters. Your Positioning Deck Has 40 Slides.
subtitle: OpenAI opened Business Hub on November 10. Everyone is writing claim-your-profile checklists. The bigger job is deciding which 300 characters ChatGPT gets to quote.
body_html:
Hmm. Remember the first time someone asked you to explain your product "in one line"? At a Diwali party, probably, somewhere between the sweets and the card table. You gave them three lines, one "basically," and a "but honestly it's more than that."

OpenAI is now asking the same question. With a character counter.

On November 10, OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT in beta. Through Business Hub, a company can claim its profile, get verified, update key details, add product feeds with pricing, and see how people engage with it inside ChatGPT. OpenAI puts the audience at 1.2 billion weekly users. Eligible US ecommerce and online service businesses can also build a Business Agent, a labelled chat that answers buyer questions on your behalf.

Most of the coverage so far reads like a Google Business Profile checklist. Add the DNS record, pick a category, verify your ID, done. Fair enough. Claiming is free and the review takes a few days, so yes, go do it.

But tucked inside the flow is a box. Index Lab, which claimed its own profile the day after launch, describes it: "More about your business," free text, 300 characters, and ChatGPT can share it in conversations when it's relevant.

Aah. So that's where your positioning lives now.

Not the homepage hero your designer fought for. Not the 40-slide messaging deck. Three hundred characters, roughly two tweets, that a chatbot may quote to a buyer who is comparing you with two competitors. In my news-desk years we called this the standfirst, and editors spent longer on it than on the story. They were right.

ChatGPT, handing you 300 characters for a product your team explains in 40 slides.

Here's the part I think SaaS teams will miss. Who fills in that box?

At most companies, "claim our profile" lands with whoever owns Google Business Profile. Usually SEO, sometimes an agency, occasionally an intern with a calendar reminder. Positioning sits with product marketing. Those two people may not have spoken since the last rebrand.

Every team, when someone asks who owns the ChatGPT profile.

And the timing matters. Gartner said on November 9 that 61% of CMOs have adapted content to be more machine-readable, but only 42% have taken steps to monitor and correct misinformation about their brand in AI output. So most teams are writing for the machine. Fewer are checking what the machine says back.

Two more details worth reading slowly.

First, claiming is not a ranking boost. The launch guides say it plainly: being recommended still depends on what the rest of the web says about you. The profile fixes facts. It doesn't make ChatGPT like you more.

Second, the dashboard. Business Hub shows mentions, website clicks, and "discovery topics," which OpenAI describes as common themes across conversations where your website is cited. You don't get individual conversations, and nothing shows until you cross a privacy threshold. Still, that's a blurry but free window into what buyers ask when your name comes up. Ahem, that's voice-of-customer research. Delivered to a dashboard most PMMs won't have a login for.

What I'd do this week

  1. Claim the profile now if you're eligible. The review takes a few days, and insights only start after verification. Every day you wait is a day without your own numbers.

  2. Give the 300-character box an owner in product marketing. SEO can do the plumbing. PMM writes the words: what you are in the terms buyers use, who it's for, and one proof point. No slogans. Every character should carry a fact.

  3. Make it match everywhere else. Homepage hero, About page, G2 profile, LinkedIn company page. If your 300 characters say "for mid-market finance teams" and your homepage says "for teams of every size," the machine has to pick. Don't make it pick.

  4. Put discovery topics on the monthly PMM review. Treat them as a rough signal, not a survey. If a theme keeps showing up that your messaging ignores, that's a gap. Or a segment you didn't know you had.

  5. Keep asking the engines yourself. The dashboard gives you counts and themes, not the competitors sitting next to you in the answer. A monthly set of 20 real buyer prompts still earns its place.

What I'm watching

Whether Business Agents open up to B2B SaaS beyond US ecommerce and online services. The moment a buyer can ask "your" agent about SSO pricing inside ChatGPT, sales, support and legal will all want a say in what it's allowed to answer. And whether Google and Perplexity ship their own claim-your-business dashboards for AI answers. I'd bet on yes.

Your turn

If ChatGPT could quote only 300 characters about your product to a buyer today, which 300 would you want it to be? Hit reply. I read every one.

Cheers,

Dheeraj

Sources: OpenAI, "Introducing Businesses in ChatGPT," November 10, 2026 (https://openai.com/index/introducing-businesses-chatgpt); Barry Schwartz, Search Engine Land, "ChatGPT Business Hub is now live," November 10, 2026 (https://searchengineland.com/chatgpt-business-hub-is-now-live-501350); Index Lab, "How to claim your business on ChatGPT," November 11, 2026 (https://www.indexlab.ai/blog/claim-your-business-on-chatgpt); Gartner, "Gartner Survey Finds 42% of CMOs Are Monitoring Brand Misinformation in AI-Generated Content," November 9, 2026 (https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-11-09-gartner-survey-finds-42-percent-of-cmos-are-monitoring-brand-misinformation-in-ai-generated-content).

title: LinkedIn Just Hired a Bouncer. Your Launch Post Isn't on the List.
subtitle: On October 8, LinkedIn said its AI-slop classifier now checks every post that travels beyond your first-degree network. That's the exact door SaaS distribution walks through.
body_html:
Monday, 10:02 AM. Your launch post goes live. "We're thrilled to announce..." Within the hour, 30 colleagues reshare it, each with a slightly different AI-polished caption. Some tool drops "Great insights!" underneath. By lunch it has 41 likes, and every single one came from someone in your Slack workspace.

Ahem. Welcome to The Overlooked Memo, Issue 03, where I read the boring engineering posts so you don't have to.

This week's boring engineering post came from Tim Jurka, LinkedIn's VP of Engineering, on October 8. He explained how LinkedIn hunts "AI slop." Most coverage treated it as a cute feed-cleanup story. Thanos joke, move on.

Look, read the one sentence that matters. LinkedIn has "expanded our classifiers to cover all posts that are distributed beyond your immediate network with 94% precision at detecting AI-slop."

Beyond your immediate network. Hmm.

That's the toll booth for B2B distribution. Your first-degree connections were always going to see some of your stuff. Everything that makes LinkedIn worth a marketing budget (the second-degree reach, the stranger who turns into a lead, the post that escapes your bubble) now goes past a model first.

LinkedIn's classifier, standing between your launch post and anyone you haven't met yet.

And what does the model look at? Jurka says LinkedIn runs AI agents, each tied to a policy, checking things like "whether a post is promotional, celebrates an achievement, or is timely." Aah. Promotional, achievement, timely. That's every SaaS launch post ever written. The funding post. The G2 badge.

LinkedIn has its reasons. Pangram's July 2026 analysis, reported by Fortune, flagged more than 40% of long-form LinkedIn posts as fully AI-generated, and LinkedIn made up nearly two-thirds of everything Pangram flagged across platforms. Then CPO Hari Srinivasan said more than 1 million people clicked the "seems like AI slop" button in its first two weeks, and views of classified slop fell 40% by August. So your audience is now labeling your content for the model. Fun, no?

Who's actually exposed

Not the guy posting AI poems about cold outreach. Nobody will miss him. The exposure sits with the stuff SaaS teams built on purpose.

Employee advocacy, first. Most SaaS teams I've worked with run it the same way: marketing writes one post, AI spins 30 "personal" versions, everyone posts at 10 AM. To a system trained to catch generic and repetitive, that's a pattern. A very easy one.

The classifier, reviewing your employee advocacy kit.

Then founder-led content at scale. Three ghostwritten posts a week, same hook shape, same "here's what I learned" ending. If a model can learn your founder's voice, another model can learn the template, yeah.

And comment tools. Fortune reported in July that LinkedIn had already blocked billions of automated comment attempts. Billions. With a b.

One more thing nobody's doing the math on. 94% precision means roughly 6 of every 100 flagged posts aren't slop at all. Which human posts look most machine-made? The polished, committee-approved ones. I edited news copy for years, and honestly, half the press releases I fixed back then would get flagged today. Zero AI involved. Just a lot of stakeholders.

LinkedIn keeps saying using AI is fine. What it's hunting is sameness. That lands hardest on teams that used AI to scale output instead of scaling a point of view. Remember my running complaint about AI time savings turning into more output instead of more pipeline? Now the output gets filtered before it ever gets near pipeline. Neat. (Not neat.)

What I'd do this week

  • Pull your last 10 company and exec posts, cover the logo, and read them out loud. If any competitor could have posted them, rewrite them.

  • Retire the 30-caption advocacy kit. Send people one real fact and one question, and let them write a sentence in their own words, typos included.

  • Switch off any auto-comment tool. Yes, that one.

  • Watch how far posts travel beyond your followers, not just total impressions. If totals hold while outside reach sags, you've met the bouncer.

What I'm watching

Whether any of this touches paid. If an employee's post gets throttled organically, will Thought Leader Ads still boost it at full price? Also, Substack partnered with Pangram in July so readers can scan posts for AI. Feel free to scan this one. The typos are mine.

Okay, quick recap. LinkedIn didn't ban AI. It hired a bouncer who has seen your template before...

Your turn: which LinkedIn format lost the most reach for you since August: launch posts, advocacy reshares or founder posts? Hit reply and tell me. I read every one.

Cheers,
Dheeraj

Stuff I read for this: Tim Jurka, "The technology behind LinkedIn's fight against AI slop" (LinkedIn, Oct 8, 2026); Social Media Today on the same post (Oct 8, 2026); Fortune on 1M+ "seems like AI slop" clicks and Pangram's data (Aug 25, 2026); Fortune on LinkedIn blocking billions of automated comment attempts (Jul 31, 2026).
